parts: Text prepared for publication in "EL Mundo del Perro" magazine, No. 357, small breeds special: Shih Tzu

Buddhism, its philosophy and the symbolism of the lion were partly responsible for the high esteem in which Lion Dogs were held in the Forbidden City. Known as Ab-bah Go-, these dogs belonged to revered individuals or royalty, and Shih Tzu were credited with a number of qualities comparable to those of Buddha.

FOREHEAD. The white marking on the forehead was seen as the centre of energy, the third eye or sixth Chakra... a symbol of the Trinity, unity of mind, universalism, salvation for all and the three mystical realms: body, mouth and mind. The positive qualities believed to emanate from Shih Tzu were intuition, optimism and vision.

TOPKNOT AND FACE. A symbolic representation of all forms of artistic creativity, mysticism, charm, magical powers, wisdom and love. The luxuriant hair covering the Shih Tzu's head and face symbolises the sun's rays and the sacred Adumbara flower, which blooms once every 3,000 years.

COLLAR. The Shih Tzu's white neck and chest symbolise Buddha's flowing mantle of dignity. This mantle grants its wearer, as custodian of the sun, moon and stars, the privilege of upholding purity, justice and virtue. The rosary of Kuan Yin, Goddess of Mercy and Compassion, and the three rings of Buddha form a mantle.

COAT. The Shih Tzu's flowing coat symbolises light, strength and courage. Followers of Buddha must never reject their children, their parents, those who love them or those they have loved; otherwise, they will never attain Nirvana. Like Buddha, the Shih Tzu was regarded as a guardian of wisdom, helping everyone overcome their imperfections.

BACK. A marking may appear in the middle of the back, or extend from the upper back to its rear or close to the tip of the tail. This blanket or saddle effect symbolises the seat or blanket on which Buddha sits as minister of the sun, moon and stars. It symbolised the three forms of learning that lead to wisdom: discipline, knowledge and meditation. The Shih Tzu is said to carry a rider through the air to attain material wealth and jewels.

TAIL. The richly feathered tail, arching gracefully over the back, represents one of the five Royal Insignia attributed to anointed, or chosen, kings and holy men. This umbrella-like feature symbolises Buddha's canopy, which covers his body and protects him from the imperfections of the world.
FEET. Considered reminiscent of Buddha's jewel-embroidered shoes, which could carry their wearer 100 miles without fatigue and allow them to glide over water without getting their feet wet.
